newsitem.title: USA: Jones team subpoenas ex-White House employee.
newsitem.headline: Jones team subpoenas ex-White House employee.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's lawyer said on Thursday that attorneys for Paula Jones were trying to "embarrass and humiliate" Clinton by seeking to compel a statement from a former White House employee.

"This is obviously a behind-the-scenes effort by plaintiff's counsel to embarrass and humiliate the president by placing untrue stories in the press," said a statement issued by Robert Bennett, attorney for Clinton in Jones' sexual harassment suit against Clinton.

Jones' attorneys on Wednesday subpoenaed Kathleen Willey, a former employee in the offices of the White House counsel and social secretary, to give a sworn deposition in the suit, the head of Jones' legal fund said on Thursday.
"This is one of the legal manoeuvres" in the case, said Cindy Hays, director of the Paula Jones Legal Defence Fund.

In an interview with CNN, Dan Gecker, a lawyer from Richmond, Virginia, who represents Willey, said his client was "outraged that she has been pulled into the Paula Jones case and that her privacy and personal rights have been violated."

"She does not know Paula Jones and does not have any information that would be relevant to her. Mrs. Willey did work in the White House. She had and continues to have a very good relationship with the president," Gecker said.
The lawyer added that he would move on Willey's behalf to quash the subpoena, which demands that she be interviewed under oath by Jones' lawyers on Aug. 14.
Willey was appointed by Clinton to the board of governors of the United Service Organisation in September 1996.
The CBS television network and the Washington Times have reported that Jones' lawyers believe Willey may have information regarding possible improper sexual advances toward her by Clinton.
Bennett said, "Ms. Willey, who was employed at the White House, has absolutely no knowledge or information of any relevance regarding Paula Jones or her allegations."
Hays declined to discuss the specific aim of the subpoena, and Willey's attorney did not immediately return calls seeking comment.
Jones has accused Clinton of using his position as Arkansas governor to try to pressure Jones to agree to a request by him for sex at a Little Rock hotel in May 1991.
Clinton's lawyers have tried to postpone the lawsuit until after he leaves the White House, arguing that it would distract him from his presidential duties.

Earlier this month, Clinton's lawyers flatly denied all Jones' allegations and asked U.S. District Judge Susan Webber Wright in Little Rock to postpone the discovery process in the case until she ruled on the dismissal motion.

"What is particularly offensive is that plaintiff's counsel have done this in an attempt to pre-empt the court, which has not yet ruled on the appropriate scope and nature of discovery in this case," Bennett said.
